name: Pale Brown
lede: Pale brown is a descriptive phrase more than a name: Paterson and St Clair use it to define caramel, cognac, dust and café au lait.

sections.title: A phrase more than a name
sections.body: Paterson's dictionary uses *pale brown* to define other colors: *caramel* is a pale brown, the color of toasted sugar; *cognac* is a pale brown, like the brandy; and *dust-coloured* means the pale brown of dust [1]. St Clair's glossary does the same for *café au lait*, a pale brown like coffee mixed with milk [2]. So the phrase is a shared yardstick, and the named shades ([[caramel]], [[beige]], [[tan]]) are the specific things it points at [1][2].

sections.title: The pale brown of mourning
sections.body: Finlay records a mourning custom in Persia: the color of grief there was the pale brown of withered leaves, while Armenians mourned in sky blue and many Asian cultures wore white [3]. The point in that passage is that mourning has no single color across the world [3].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The swatch here is #755C49, which most people would call a medium brown on a screen, darker than the name suggests [4]. That gap is a reason to treat *pale* as relative: it means lighter than the brown a writer had in mind, not a fixed lightness [1][4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In the ColorHub archive, 3,814 of 23,781 paintings, about 16%, hold this color across at least 5% of the canvas, as photographed [4]. The rate is highest for the 1270s, at roughly three times the archive's average, and it runs high in works from Nepal, Korea and Tibet [4]. Among European painters, Andre Derain has 12 matching canvases and Martinus Rorbye 11 [4]. Most matches are mid-tones, with about a fifth in shadows [4].

origin.source: Paterson, A Dictionary of Colour; St Clair, The Secret Lives of Colour
